readings.title: An Encounter — part 1: doors of escape
readings.challenge: Separate the adventure the narrator imagines from the day he actually has.
readings.focus: Escape through stories, and the gap between romance and an ordinary day.
readings.context: From Joyce’s Dubliners (1914), fifteen stories of Dublin life around 1900. A boy at a Catholic college tells of playing truant. The Union Jack, Pluck and The Halfpenny Marvel were cheap boys’ papers; miching means playing truant; National School boys attended the free state schools; the Pigeon House was a fort and power station at the mouth of the river Liffey. A bob is a shilling and a tanner sixpence. “Swaddlers” was a slang term for Protestants.
readings.contentNote: The boys’ games imitate Wild West stereotypes of Native Americans, and the narrator refers to a fellow passenger as “a little Jew with a bag”; these belong to the story’s world and period.

excerpt.locator: An Encounter, from the opening through the abandoned walk to the Pigeon House; opens “It was Joe Dillon who introduced the Wild West to us. He had a little library made up of…”; closes “…in behind some clouds and left us to our jaded thoughts and the crumbs of our provisions.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator join the Wild West games, and what does he say the stories gave him?
facilitatorNotes: He is one of the “reluctant Indians,” afraid of seeming studious or weak. The adventures are remote from his nature, but they “opened doors of escape.” He wants a way out more than he wants the stories themselves.
evidence: the reluctant Indians who were afraid to seem studious or lacking in robustness, I was one
they opened doors of escape

questions.prompt: What does Father Butler’s rebuke reveal about the school’s values beyond disapproval of cheap reading?
facilitatorNotes: He contrasts “boys like you, educated” with National School boys, so the offence is partly against class standing. The rebuke still awakens “one of my consciences” in the narrator: he notices Leo Dillon’s confused face.
evidence: I could understand it if you were . . . National School boys.
the confused puffy face of Leo Dillon awakened one of my consciences

questions.prompt: How does the day measure up to the narrator’s idea that real adventures “must be sought abroad”?
facilitatorNotes: They see ships and foreign sailors and imagine geography taking substance, but they never reach the Pigeon House, and the day ends with tiredness and crumbs. His search for green-eyed sailors is a private notion he cannot explain. The romance keeps shrinking into the ordinary.
evidence: real adventures, I reflected, do not happen to people who remain at home: they must be sought abroad
left us to our jaded thoughts and the crumbs of our provisions

readings.title: An Encounter — part 2: the man in the field
readings.challenge: Infer what the narrator does not name from what he notices and avoids looking at.
readings.focus: An adult’s menace felt through repetition, and a boy’s shame at his own pride.
readings.context: Recap: the narrator and Mahony have played truant, wandered the docks and Ringsend, and given up on reaching the Pigeon House. They rest in a field. A josser is an old fellow; Thomas Moore, Walter Scott and Lord Lytton were popular nineteenth-century writers.
readings.contentNote: A stranger’s predatory talk with two boys, an implied act of indecency and a fixation on whipping; nothing explicit is described.

excerpt.locator: An Encounter, from the old man’s approach to the end of the story; opens “There was nobody but ourselves in the field. When we had lain on the bank for some time…”; closes “…to bring me aid. And I was penitent; for in my heart I had always despised him a little.”.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator’s wish to seem bookish shape his first response to the man?
facilitatorNotes: He pretends to have read every book mentioned and is pained when Mahony asks a naive question, afraid the man will think him as stupid as Mahony. His vanity draws him into the man’s confidence and separates him from his friend.
evidence: I pretended that I had read every book he mentioned
I was afraid the man would think I was as stupid as Mahony

questions.prompt: How does Joyce convey the man’s disturbance without describing his actions directly?
facilitatorNotes: Through the narrator’s impressions of repetition and circling speech, and through Mahony’s exclamation, which the narrator neither answers nor looks up at. The story gives the effect of the man’s mind and leaves the act unnamed.
evidence: his mind was slowly circling round and round in the same orbit
As I neither answered nor raised my eyes

questions.prompt: The narrator once looked for sailors with green eyes. What is the effect of meeting “bottle-green eyes” here?
facilitatorNotes: The adventure he imagined arrives in a frightening form: the strange figure he half sought is a menacing adult. The echo links romantic longing to danger and turns the day’s quest back on him.
evidence: I met the gaze of a pair of bottle-green eyes peering at me from under a twitching forehead

questions.prompt: Why is the narrator “penitent” at the end?
facilitatorNotes: He is ashamed of his “paltry stratagem” of false names and of his forced bravery, and he recognizes that Mahony, whom he secretly despised, runs to him as if to help. The encounter exposes his own pride as well as the man’s menace.
evidence: I was ashamed of my paltry stratagem
And I was penitent; for in my heart I had always despised him a little.

readings.title: After the Race
readings.challenge: Hear how the narration borrows Jimmy’s excitement while letting the reader see more than he does.
readings.focus: Money, nationality and a young man’s wish to belong among the wealthy.
readings.context: From Joyce’s Dubliners (1914), fifteen stories of Dublin life around 1900. In 1903 the Gordon Bennett Cup, an international motor race, was run in Ireland. Jimmy Doyle, son of a rich Dublin butcher, rides home with Continental friends. Kingstown is a harbour town south of Dublin; Cadet Roussel is a French song; an I.O.U. is a written promise to pay.

excerpt.locator: After the Race; complete individual work; opens “The cars came scudding in towards Dublin, running evenly like pellets in the groove of…”; closes “"Daybreak, gentlemen!"”.

questions.prompt: What does the opening paragraph suggest about the Irish spectators and the visiting cars?
facilitatorNotes: The wealth and industry of the Continent speed through “this channel of poverty and inaction,” and the crowd cheers like the “gratefully oppressed.” The irony frames Irish onlookers as admirers of power they do not share.
evidence: through this channel of poverty and inaction the Continent sped its wealth and industry
the cheer of the gratefully oppressed

questions.prompt: How do Jimmy’s father’s history and Jimmy’s knowledge of money raise the stakes of the evening?
facilitatorNotes: The father modified his Nationalist views, made money through shops and police contracts, and is now a “merchant prince.” Jimmy knows how hard the money was got together, yet he is about to stake most of it to belong among Ségouin’s set.
evidence: His father, who had begun life as an advanced Nationalist, had modified his views early.
knew well with what difficulty it had been got together

questions.prompt: How do sentences like “It must have been a good speech” reveal the limits of Jimmy’s understanding?
facilitatorNotes: The narration takes on his excited, uncertain point of view; he is unsure what he said, who is winning, or even which cards he holds. The exclamations sound like his enthusiasm while showing that he is being carried along.
evidence: It must have been a good speech.
Jimmy did not know exactly who was winning but he knew that he was losing.

questions.prompt: Who wins the last game and who loses, and why might the ending be read politically?
facilitatorNotes: The game lies between Routh, the Englishman, and Ségouin, the Frenchman; Jimmy and the American Farley lose most. Villona, the poor Hungarian who did not play, announces daybreak. Some readers see Ireland’s position among richer nations; others read a simpler moral of a young man’s folly. Both can use the closing details.
evidence: Jimmy understood that the game lay between Routh and Ségouin.
glad of the dark stupor that would cover up his folly

readings.title: Two Gallants — part 1: a walk and a plan
readings.challenge: Work out an unstated plan from what two men say and avoid saying.
readings.focus: Flattery, dependence and the treatment of a young woman as a resource.
readings.context: From Joyce’s Dubliners (1914), fifteen stories of Dublin life around 1900. Two men in their late twenties walk through Dublin on a Sunday evening. A gallant is a fashionable man attentive to women; a slavey is a servant girl; racing tissues are betting tips; a Lothario is a seducer; “on the turf” here means working as a prostitute.
readings.contentNote: Crude slang about women, the sexual and financial exploitation of a young servant, and a woman said to have turned to prostitution.

excerpt.locator: Two Gallants, from the opening through the walk to Kildare Street; opens “The grey warm evening of August had descended upon the city and a mild warm air, a memory…”; closes “"She's a fine decent tart," he said, with appreciation; "that's what she is."”.

questions.prompt: How does the description of Lenehan undercut the youthful image his clothes present?
facilitatorNotes: Breeches, white shoes and a jaunty waterproof “expressed youth,” but his waist, scant grey hair and ravaged face tell a different story. He is acting a part he has outgrown.
evidence: His breeches, his white rubber shoes and his jauntily slung waterproof expressed youth.
had a ravaged look

questions.prompt: What has Corley received from the young woman so far, and what does he hide from her?
facilitatorNotes: She brings him cigarettes, pays his tram fare and once gave him two cigars from her employer. He has hidden his name and lied about his job. The relationship is already one in which he takes.
evidence: Cigarettes every night she'd bring me and paying the tram out and back.
She doesn't know my name.

questions.prompt: Why does Lenehan leave his flattery “open to the interpretation of raillery”?
facilitatorNotes: He depends on Corley and must please him, but mocking undertones let him keep some self-respect. Corley, not subtle, takes the praise straight. The sentence shows a parasite managing his own servility.
evidence: A shade of mockery relieved the servility of his manner.
To save himself he had the habit of leaving his flattery open to the interpretation of raillery.

readings.title: Two Gallants — part 2: the gold coin
readings.challenge: Follow Lenehan alone for most of the evening and read what the final gesture reveals.
readings.focus: Loneliness, appetite and the meaning of a small gold coin.
readings.context: Recap: Lenehan, a hanger-on, walks with Corley, who boasts of a servant girl who gives him gifts and believes he is respectable; Lenehan anxiously asks whether Corley can “pull it off.” The harp is an emblem of Ireland, and “Silent, O Moyle” is a Thomas Moore song of a king’s daughter turned into a swan. “A little of the ready” means some ready money.
readings.contentNote: Implied sexual and financial exploitation of a young servant woman.

excerpt.locator: Two Gallants, from the harpist in Kildare Street to the end of the story; opens “They walked along Nassau Street and then turned into Kildare Street. Not far from the…”; closes “…opened it slowly to the gaze of his disciple. A small gold coin shone in the palm.”.

questions.prompt: How might the harpist and his harp comment on the young woman and on Ireland?
facilitatorNotes: The harp is weary of strangers’ eyes and her master’s hands, her covering fallen about her knees. The image of a used, exposed instrument anticipates the servant girl and suggests a nation played upon by others.
evidence: His harp, too, heedless that her coverings had fallen about her knees, seemed weary alike of the eyes of strangers and of her master's hands.

questions.prompt: What does Lenehan long for in the refreshment bar, and how does the way he imagines it limit the longing?
facilitatorNotes: He wants a home, a warm fire and a good dinner; he feels his “poverty of purse and spirit.” Yet he imagines getting it through a “simple-minded girl” with money, repeating Corley’s calculation in a gentler key.
evidence: This vision made him feel keenly his own poverty of purse and spirit.
if he could only come across some good simple-minded girl with a little of the ready

questions.prompt: Why does the story withhold what Corley wanted until the last sentence, and what does “disciple” suggest?
facilitatorNotes: The reader, like Lenehan, assumes a sexual conquest; the coin reveals that the aim was money, probably taken from her employer. “Disciple” turns Lenehan into a follower before a mock revelation. The title’s “gallants” becomes bitterly ironic.
evidence: opened it slowly to the gaze of his disciple
A small gold coin shone in the palm.

readings.title: Counterparts — part 1: the copy and the retort
readings.challenge: Track the pressures that build in Farrington across an afternoon at work.
readings.focus: Humiliation, thirst and a moment of wit that changes nothing.
readings.context: From Joyce’s Dubliners (1914), fifteen stories of Dublin life around 1900. Farrington is a copying clerk in a solicitors’ office, writing out legal documents by hand. A g.p. is a glass of plain porter; a curate here is a barman; a snug is a small private room in a pub; an order on the cashier is an advance on wages.
readings.contentNote: Workplace bullying and drinking; a client is described as “of Jewish appearance,” a dated stereotype in the narration.

excerpt.locator: Counterparts, from the opening through Mr. Alleyne’s threat after the retort; opens “The bell rang furiously and, when Miss Parker went to the tube, a furious voice called…”; closes “…quit the office instanter! You'll quit this, I'm telling you, or you'll apologise to me!"”.

questions.prompt: How do the bodies of Farrington and Mr. Alleyne set up their conflict?
facilitatorNotes: Farrington is tall, heavy and wine-faced; Alleyne is a little man with an egg-like, hairless head. Farrington stares at the “polished skull,” “gauging its fragility”: physical strength confronts social power.
evidence: The man stared fixedly at the polished skull which directed the affairs of Crosbie & Alleyne, gauging its fragility.

questions.prompt: What does the unfinished legal sentence show about Farrington’s afternoon?
facilitatorNotes: He stares at “In no case shall the said Bernard Bodley be . . .,” notices the alliteration, and finally writes “Bernard Bernard.” His work stalls on a formula of prohibition while his thirst and rage take over.
evidence: thought how strange it was that the last three words began with the same letter
he wrote Bernard Bernard instead of Bernard Bodley and had to begin again on a clean sheet

questions.prompt: Is the retort a triumph or a disaster for Farrington?
facilitatorNotes: It is a brilliant answer to a trap question, found “almost before he was aware of it,” and it astonishes even its author. But it gives Alleyne grounds to demand an apology or dismissal. The wit wins the moment and loses the position.
evidence: almost before he was aware of it, his tongue had found a felicitous moment
You'll apologise to me for your impertinence or you'll quit the office instanter!

readings.title: Counterparts — part 2: rounds and a beating
readings.challenge: Follow the evening’s gains and losses and see how the last scene repeats the first.
readings.focus: Humiliation passed down from master to clerk to child.
readings.context: Recap: Farrington, a clerk who drinks, failed to finish a copy, was berated by his employer Mr. Alleyne, and answered him with a cutting retort before the whole office. A pawn-office lends money against goods; a crown is five shillings; a half-one and small hot specials are whiskeys; Apollinaris is mineral water; the Tivoli was a music hall.
readings.contentNote: Heavy drinking and sexual leering; the story ends with a father beating his young son with a stick.

excerpt.locator: Counterparts, from the section break after the office scene to the end of the story; opens “. . . . . . . .”; closes “…say a Hail Mary for you, pa, if you don't beat me. . . . I'll say a Hail Mary. . . ."”.

questions.prompt: How does the retort change as Farrington prepares and tells it?
facilitatorNotes: He composes the narration in advance, adding coolness and timing (“taking my time, you know”) and a slightly altered wording. Higgins later performs it too. The retort becomes a pub story whose value lies in the telling.
evidence: As he walked on he preconsidered the terms in which he would narrate the incident to the boys:
Then I looked back at him again—taking my time, you know.

questions.prompt: Why is it ironic that Farrington hates “a sponge”?
facilitatorNotes: He has pawned his watch and stood rounds to win admiration, and he has thought of borrowing from Pat and Higgins. Resenting Weathers for accepting drinks shows his generosity was a purchase of status. The line exposes his self-deception.
evidence: If there was one thing that he hated it was a sponge.

questions.prompt: How does the arm-wrestling match repeat the office scene?
facilitatorNotes: Called on to uphold the national honour, he is beaten twice by a “stripling,” as earlier a small man mastered him by rank. His fury again finds no proper target and turns on the barman.
evidence: Farrington's dark wine-coloured face flushed darker still with anger and humiliation at having been defeated by such a stripling.
What the hell do you know about it?

questions.prompt: What does the title “Counterparts” mean once you reach the last scene?
facilitatorNotes: A counterpart is a duplicate copy of a legal document, Farrington’s trade, and also a person who mirrors another. He mimics his son’s accent as he once mimicked Alleyne’s, and bullies the weaker as he was bullied; his wife and he bully each other in turn. The boy’s offer of a Hail Mary is a plea for mercy that the story leaves unanswered.
evidence: He began to mimic his son's flat accent
I'll say a Hail Mary for you, pa, if you don't beat me.

readings.title: A Mother — part 1: a contract for four concerts
readings.challenge: Notice how the narrator’s phrasing judges Mrs. Kearney before the plot gives her anything to do.
readings.focus: Ambition, respectability and a contract in the world of the Irish Revival.
readings.context: From Joyce’s Dubliners (1914), fifteen stories of Dublin life around 1900. Mr. Holohan is assistant secretary of the Eire Abu Society, a nationalist cultural society. The Irish Revival promoted the Irish language and culture; the name Kathleen recalls Cathleen Ni Houlihan, a traditional figure for Ireland. Skerries, Howth and Greystones are seaside places near Dublin. The Antient Concert Rooms were a Dublin hall; a guinea was a pound and a shilling; a house “filled with paper” is filled with free tickets.

excerpt.locator: A Mother, from the opening through the cancelled Friday concert; opens “Mr. Holohan, assistant secretary of the Eire Abu Society, had been walking up and down…”; closes “…a male. She was glad that he had suggested coming with her. She thought her plans over.”.

questions.prompt: “Miss Devlin had become Mrs. Kearney out of spite.” What does the rest of the paragraph explain, and how does the narrator’s tone treat her?
facilitatorNotes: Unbending and proud, she waited for a brilliant suitor, consoled herself with Turkish Delight in secret, and married a much older bootmaker when friends began to gossip. Phrases like “the chilly circle of her accomplishments” are ironic, close to mocking. Some readers find the tone unfair to a woman with few choices; the same details also show how few choices she had.
evidence: She sat amid the chilly circle of her accomplishments, waiting for some suitor to brave it and offer her a brilliant life.
she silenced them by marrying Mr. Kearney, who was a bootmaker on Ormond Quay.

questions.prompt: How does Mrs. Kearney use the Irish Revival?
facilitatorNotes: She “determined to take advantage of her daughter's name,” hires an Irish teacher, and joins a circle that exchanges Irish postcards and says good-bye in Irish. The revival is a route to standing as much as a cause. The satire falls on the fashionable side of the movement as well as on her.
evidence: Mrs. Kearney determined to take advantage of her daughter's name and brought an Irish teacher to the house.
said good-bye to one another in Irish

questions.prompt: Compare Mrs. Kearney with Mr. Holohan and Mr. Fitzpatrick. Who is competent, and how does the narrator show it?
facilitatorNotes: Holohan walks up and down and makes notes, “but in the end it was Mrs. Kearney who arranged everything”; she knows how to word bills and order a programme. Fitzpatrick has a vacant smile and chews his programme to pulp. She does the work while the men hold the authority.
evidence: but in the end it was Mrs. Kearney who arranged everything.
he chewed one end of it into a moist pulp

questions.prompt: Why does she not ask “And who is the Cometty pray?”, and what does her view of her husband as being like the General Post Office suggest about her position?
facilitatorNotes: It would not be ladylike, so she keeps silent. She values her husband as “something large, secure and fixed,” for his “abstract value as a male”: his presence may carry weight that her words do not. Readers can take this as satire of her snobbery or as a picture of the limits she works within; it can be both.
evidence: But she knew that it would not be ladylike to do that: so she was silent.
she appreciated his abstract value as a male.

readings.title: A Mother — part 2: the night of the grand concert
readings.challenge: Watch how each new character is drawn in a few details, and what those details say about Dublin’s musical world.
readings.focus: Small vanities among the performers, and a demand that begins to set Mrs. Kearney apart.
readings.context: Recap: Mrs. Kearney arranged for her daughter Kathleen to accompany four concerts of the Eire Abu Society for eight guineas. The first concerts were thinly attended and the Friday concert was cancelled; suspicious of the committee, she has brought her husband on Saturday. The Feis Ceoil is an Irish music festival; Maritana is a popular opera; Mrs. Pat Campbell was a famous actress; the Freeman is the Freeman’s Journal, a Dublin newspaper.
readings.contentNote: A newspaperman’s leering view of a young woman.

excerpt.locator: A Mother, from the Saturday arrival to the Freeman man’s drink upstairs; opens “The night of the grand concert came. Mrs. Kearney, with her husband and daughter, arrived…”; closes “…upon which he balanced the fine problem of his finances. He was widely respected.”.

questions.prompt: How does Miss Beirne’s face change as she looks at the rain, and why might Joyce include her?
facilitatorNotes: The melancholy of the wet street wipes away her trustfulness and enthusiasm, and she sighs that they did their best. She stands for the society’s hopeful amateur effort, which Mrs. Kearney meets with a curt “No, thank you!”
evidence: She looked out at the rain until the melancholy of the wet street effaced all the trustfulness and enthusiasm from her twisted features.
Ah, well! We did our best, the dear knows.

questions.prompt: Choose two of the performers (Mr. Duggan, Mr. Bell, Madam Glynn). Which details make each comic or pitiable?
facilitatorNotes: Duggan rose from a hall porter’s son to grand opera but wipes his nose in his gloved hand; Bell won a bronze medal on his fourth try and hides jealousy under friendliness; Madam Glynn, in a faded dress, is caught by a shadow that falls “revengefully” on her collar-bone. The precision can feel cruel or compassionate; readers may disagree about which.
evidence: he marred the good impression by wiping his nose in his gloved hand once or twice out of thoughtlessness
On his fourth trial he had been awarded a bronze medal.
The shadow took her faded dress into shelter but fell revengefully into the little cup behind her collar-bone.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Kearney says she has her contract. What do Mr. Holohan’s replies show about how the society is run?
facilitatorNotes: Each official passes the obligation to someone else: Holohan says Fitzpatrick has charge of payment and that it is not his business. Her claim is sound; the question the story raises is how others will judge her manner of pressing it.
evidence: Mr. Holohan said that it wasn't his business.
I have my contract, and I intend to see that it is carried out.

questions.prompt: What do Mr. Hendrick and Mr. O’Madden Burke add to the story? Look closely at the “moral umbrella.”
facilitatorNotes: The press that will review the concert does not stay for it, and Hendrick takes Miss Healy’s politeness as tribute to himself. Burke balances his finances on his imposing name and is “widely respected.” These are the men whose judgement of Mrs. Kearney will count, and the narration has already shown how much their respectability is worth.
evidence: His magniloquent western name was the moral umbrella upon which he balanced the fine problem of his finances.
He was widely respected.

readings.title: A Mother — part 3: “I'm asking for my rights”
readings.challenge: Decide whose judgement the ending invites you to share, and whether you share it.
readings.focus: A woman’s demand for what a contract owes, and a community that closes ranks against her.
readings.context: Recap: Kathleen Kearney was engaged to accompany four concerts for eight guineas. One concert was cancelled, and on the last night her mother cannot get the secretaries to say when Kathleen will be paid; the audience is waiting. Four pounds eight shillings is half of eight guineas. Killarney is a sentimental song; “fol-the-diddle-I-do” mocks a self-important official.

excerpt.locator: A Mother, from the standoff in the dressing-room to the end of the story; opens “While Mr. Holohan was entertaining the Freeman man Mrs. Kearney was speaking so…”; closes “…proper thing, Holohan," said Mr. O'Madden Burke, poised upon his umbrella in approval.”.

questions.prompt: What does Mrs. Kearney demand before the concert can begin, and how does Kathleen behave?
facilitatorNotes: She will not let Kathleen play without her money; when Fitzpatrick pays half, she notes it is four shillings short. Kathleen looks at her shoe, “it was not her fault,” then on her own leads the first singer out. Her silence can be read as embarrassment, as obedience, or as a quiet judgement of her own.
evidence: She won't go on without her money.
This is four shillings short.
Kathleen looked down, moving the point of her new shoe: it was not her fault.

questions.prompt: “They wouldn't have dared to have treated her like that if she had been a man.” Is Mrs. Kearney right? Use evidence from the whole story.
facilitatorNotes: The baritone, a man, “had been paid his money” and wants peace, and no committee member takes responsibility for the contract. Yet her insistence also damages Kathleen’s career. A defensible reading is that she is right about the injustice and wrong in her tactics; others see the line as self-pity. The narration reports her view without endorsing it.
evidence: They wouldn't have dared to have treated her like that if she had been a man.
He had been paid his money and wished to be at peace with men.

questions.prompt: What changes after Mr. Holohan says “I thought you were a lady”?
facilitatorNotes: Argument gives way to a verdict on her conduct as a woman: “condemned on all hands.” Her mimicry of the secretaries had given her a voice; now she stands “like an angry stone image” and leaves. The charge of being unladylike wins where the contract could not be answered.
evidence: I thought you were a lady,
After that Mrs. Kearney's conduct was condemned on all hands
She stood still for an instant like an angry stone image

questions.prompt: Why might Joyce end with Mr. O’Madden Burke “poised upon his umbrella in approval” rather than with Mrs. Kearney? What does the title “A Mother” add?
facilitatorNotes: The last word goes to the man whose respectability rests on a name and an umbrella, so his approval is hollow. The title asks whether her fight is for Kathleen or for herself; the story leaves the daughter almost silent. Readers may feel relief at her exit and irony at the committee’s self-satisfaction at once.
evidence: You did the proper thing, Holohan,
poised upon his umbrella in approval.

readings.title: Grace — part 1: the fall
readings.challenge: Gather what the crowd, the constable and Mr. Power reveal about the injured man before the narrator tells his history.
readings.focus: A fall, literal and social, told with detached precision.
readings.context: From Joyce’s Dubliners (1914), fifteen stories of Dublin life around 1900. A curate here is a barman; an ulster is a long overcoat; an outsider is a two-wheeled hired car; the Ballast Office had a public clock. Mr. Power works in the Royal Irish Constabulary office at Dublin Castle, the seat of British government in Ireland. E.C. is a City of London postal district.
readings.contentNote: Drunkenness and a bloody injury, including a bitten tongue.

excerpt.locator: Grace, from the opening through Mr. Power’s departure from the Kernans’ house; opens “Two gentlemen who were in the lavatory at the time tried to lift him up: but he was quite…”; closes “. . . . . . . .”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening present the injured man before we learn his name? What is the effect?
facilitatorNotes: He is “the man,” “the injured man,” “the person on the floor,” smeared with filth, with a “dark medal of blood” by his head. The anonymous, almost clinical view makes his fall a public spectacle; “medal” is an ironic decoration.
evidence: his clothes were smeared with the filth and ooze of the floor on which he had lain, face downwards.
A dark medal of blood had formed itself near the man's head on the tessellated floor.

questions.prompt: Which details make the scene comic as well as grim?
facilitatorNotes: The constable licks his pencil and makes “ready to indite” as if he feared a delusion; the crowd “distended and closed again elastically”; Kernan insists “'s nothing” through a bitten tongue. Readers may feel sympathy and amusement at once, which suits the story’s detached tone.
evidence: licked the lead of his pencil and made ready to indite
The ring of onlookers distended and closed again elastically.

questions.prompt: What do the silk hat and gaiters mean to Mr. Kernan, and how does his position compare with Mr. Power’s?
facilitatorNotes: By grace of them a man could always “pass muster”: appearance is dignity. His hat is now dinged and battered. Power’s rise and Kernan’s decline are “arcs” that cross. The phrase “By grace of” gives the title’s word its first, worldly sense.
evidence: By grace of these two articles of clothing, he said, a man could always pass muster.
The arc of his social rise intersected the arc of his friend's decline

questions.prompt: Mr. Power promises, “We'll make a new man of him.” What does the scene at the Kernans’ house suggest about that promise?
facilitatorNotes: Power notices the children’s manners and accents with a thoughtful brow; Mrs. Kernan says her husband has been drinking since Friday and does not think he has a home. Power’s promise is cheerful and made “gaily.” “A new man” echoes the Christian language of conversion; the story will test whether anything so deep is on offer.
evidence: He was surprised at their manners and at their accents, and his brow grew thoughtful.
He's been drinking since Friday.
We'll make a new man of him,

readings.title: Grace — part 2: friends at the bedside
readings.challenge: Track the plan the friends keep from Mr. Kernan, and how each man’s history shapes what he says.
readings.focus: Marriage, respectability, and a conversation steered by a capable man.
readings.context: Recap: Tom Kernan, a commercial traveller in decline, fell drunk down the stairs of a bar and bit his tongue. His friend Mr. Power brought him home and promised Mrs. Kernan that his friends would make a new man of him. The Sacred Heart is a Catholic devotion; the banshee is a spirit of Irish folklore. Peloothered means drunk; bostooms are louts; omadhauns are fools. Bona-fide travellers could buy drink on Sunday outside the city. “65, catch your cabbage” is a joke about drilling country recruits to the police.
readings.contentNote: The narration reports the men’s antisemitic contempt for a moneylender, including a slur on his disabled son; heavy drinking and an unhappy marriage.

excerpt.locator: Grace, from Mrs. Kernan’s watching the car out of sight to the friends’ plan to meet on Thursday; opens “Mrs. Kernan's puzzled eyes watched the car till it was out of sight. Then she withdrew…”; closes “"Half-seven at M'Auley's be it!"”.

questions.prompt: How does the paragraph on Mrs. Kernan’s marriage sum up twenty-five years? What is her religion like?
facilitatorNotes: She found a wife’s life irksome within three weeks, became a mother, and keeps house shrewdly; she accepts her husband’s drinking “as part of the climate.” Religion is a habit, “bounded by her kitchen,” with room for the banshee and the Holy Ghost alike. The tone is comic but not unkind: she is practical rather than devout.
evidence: She accepted his frequent intemperance as part of the climate
Her faith was bounded by her kitchen, but, if she was put to it, she could believe also in the banshee and in the Holy Ghost.

questions.prompt: Why is Mr. Cunningham “the very man for such a case”? Is there irony in the choice?
facilitatorNotes: He is sensible, informed by the police courts, and his friends defer to him, even thinking his face like Shakespeare’s. Yet his own wife is an incurable drunkard who has pawned their furniture six times. His authority is social, and the man sent to reform a drinker has failed to reform one at home.
evidence: He had set up house for her six times; and each time she had pawned the furniture on him.
His friends bowed to his opinions and considered that his face was like Shakespeare's.

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Kernan want the details of his evening “to remain vague,” and what does the passage about Mr. Harford reveal about the friends?
facilitatorNotes: He was abandoned by Harford and is ashamed. The friends know Harford’s drinking habits and stay silent. The narration voices their resentment of Harford as a moneylender in antisemitic terms, then notes that “at other times” they remember his good points: their contempt is prejudice that comes and goes with their debts. Discuss whether the narration shares the prejudice or exposes it.
evidence: He wished the details of the incident to remain vague.
At other times they remembered his good points.

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Power answer M'Coy’s question “as if Mr. Kernan had asked it”? What does it show about the code among these men?
facilitatorNotes: Power resents M'Coy for borrowing valises under false pretences and resents “such low playing of the game” more than the loss. The men keep finely graded rules of respectability, enforced through small snubs that the others may not even notice.
evidence: More than he resented the fact that he had been victimised he resented such low playing of the game.
He answered the question, therefore, as if Mr. Kernan had asked it.

readings.title: Grace — part 3: washing the pot
readings.challenge: Notice how the friends recruit Mr. Kernan without ever simply asking him.
readings.focus: Persuasion through talk, and religion as a matter of class and loyalty.
readings.context: Recap: Mr. Kernan is in bed after his drunken fall. His friends Power, Cunningham and M'Coy have come, with Mrs. Kernan’s blessing, to bring him back to the Catholic Church, which he joined at his marriage and has neglected for twenty years. A retreat is a series of sermons and devotions; Father Tom Burke was a famous Dominican preacher; an Orangeman belongs to a Protestant society loyal to the Crown; “the Prisoner of the Vatican” was a name for the popes after Italy took Rome in 1870.

excerpt.locator: Grace, from Mr. Kernan’s question about Thursday to the announcement of a visitor; opens “There was a short silence. Mr. Kernan waited to see whether he would be taken into his…”; closes “"Not a doubt of it," said Mr. Kernan warmly.”.

questions.prompt: How do the friends reveal the retreat, and why does Mr. Cunningham call it washing the pot?
facilitatorNotes: Cunningham is evasive (“a little . . . spiritual matter”) until Power says it point blank. The homely metaphor and “a nice collection of scoundrels” make it sound like a shared lark, and Cunningham’s sudden idea that Kernan join seems staged. Persuasion works through fellowship rather than argument.
evidence: it's just a little . . . spiritual matter.
we're all going to wash the pot.
You might join in and we'd have a four-handed reel.

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Kernan show “a stiff neck,” and what wins him over?
facilitatorNotes: He will not seem to be managed, so he listens “with an air of calm enmity.” Talk of the Jesuits flatters him: they are educated and cater for the upper classes, and that is why he has “a feeling for them.” Snobbery does what piety could not.
evidence: he thought he owed it to his dignity to show a stiff neck.
The Jesuits cater for the upper classes,
That's why I have a feeling for them.

questions.prompt: What does the talk about Father Tom Burke and Crofton suggest about what these men value in religion?
facilitatorNotes: They admire the preacher’s style and voice, and admit he was not much of a theologian. Kernan quotes an Orangeman’s tolerant remark, M'Coy half agrees, and Cunningham closes ranks: “our religion is the religion.” Religion here is performance and tribal loyalty more than belief; some readers also hear genuine warmth in the memory.
evidence: Upon my word it was magnificent, the style of the oratory.
our religion is the religion, the old, original faith.

readings.title: Grace — part 4: Credo
readings.challenge: Weigh what the friends claim to know against how confidently they claim it, and watch the mood of the room change.
readings.focus: Confident half-knowledge, and a story that produces a feeling of faith.
readings.context: Recap: Mr. Kernan’s friends have persuaded him, half against his will, to join them at a retreat for business men at the Jesuit church on Thursday. Now a grocer, Mr. Fogarty, arrives with whisky. Leo XIII was Pope from 1878 to 1903 and Pius IX before him; ex cathedra means with the full authority of the papal office; the Vatican Council declared papal infallibility in 1870. John MacHale was Archbishop of Tuam; Credo is Latin for “I believe.” At a retreat’s close the congregation renews its baptismal vows holding lighted candles.

excerpt.locator: Grace, from Mr. Fogarty’s arrival to Mr. Kernan’s refusal of the candles; opens “Mrs. Kernan came to the door of the bedroom and announced:”; closes “. . . . . . . .”.

questions.prompt: Follow the argument over Leo XIII’s motto and the German cardinal. How reliable is the friends’ knowledge, and why does it not matter to them?
facilitatorNotes: They correct one another with confidence: “Lux upon Lux,” “Lux in Tenebris,” “Tenebrae”; the cardinal is “Dolling . . . or Dowling.” Their facts are muddled (the German who refused the dogma was the theologian Döllinger, not a cardinal), but authority in this room comes from tone, and Cunningham wins by being positive.
evidence: it was Lux upon Lux.
a German cardinal by the name of Dolling . . . or Dowling

questions.prompt: How does Mr. Cunningham’s story of John MacHale change the room?
facilitatorNotes: MacHale argues against infallibility, then shouts “Credo!” the moment the Pope declares it. The words build “the vast image of the church” in the listeners’ minds, and Mrs. Kernan enters a “solemn company.” The story produces a feeling of faith whose content is submission; whether that feeling is real devotion or a mood is open to argument.
evidence: shouted out with the voice of a lion
Mr. Cunningham's words had built up the vast image of the church in the minds of his hearers.

questions.prompt: Mr. Kernan agrees to the retreat but bars the candles. What does his objection reveal?
facilitatorNotes: He accepts confession but calls the candles “magic-lantern business,” the scruple of a man of Protestant stock, and he enjoys “having created an effect on his audience.” His conversion is partly performance; his wife’s retort points the irony.
evidence: I bar the magic-lantern business.
conscious of having created an effect on his audience
There's a nice Catholic for you!

readings.title: Grace — part 5: the spiritual accountant
readings.challenge: Compare the sermon’s language with what the story has shown of the men listening to it.
readings.focus: Religion translated into business, and the irony of the story’s title.
readings.context: Recap: after his drunken fall, Tom Kernan has been talked by his friends Cunningham, Power, M'Coy and Fogarty into attending a retreat for business men. A transept is a cross-arm of a church; a quincunx is an arrangement of five, four at the corners and one in the centre; the red light before the altar marks the reserved Sacrament. Father Purdon’s text is Luke 16:8–9, the close of the parable of the unjust steward, who is praised for dealing shrewdly with his master’s debtors; Mammon is wealth thought of as a god.

excerpt.locator: Grace, the retreat at the Jesuit church in Gardiner Street, to the end of the story; opens “The transept of the Jesuit Church in Gardiner Street was almost full; and still at every…”; closes “…But, with God's grace, I will rectify this and this. I will set right my accounts."”.

questions.prompt: Who sits in the congregation around Mr. Kernan, and what does the list suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Harford the moneylender, Fanning the “mayor maker,” Grimes with his pawnbroker’s shops, a nephew up for a job, Hendrick of the Freeman, and poor O’Carroll. It is the city’s web of money and influence, and Kernan feels “more at home” as he recognises faces. The church gathers the same men the pubs and offices do.
evidence: Mr. Harford, the moneylender
Gradually, as he recognised familiar faces, Mr. Kernan began to feel more at home.

questions.prompt: How does Father Purdon interpret his text, and what is strange about his reading?
facilitatorNotes: He admits it is one of the most difficult texts, then presents the worshippers of Mammon as “exemplars” for business men and calls himself their “spiritual accountant.” A parable about a dishonest steward becomes reassurance that ordinary dealings can be squared with God. Some readers find this a hollow bargain; others say he meets his audience where they live.
evidence: It was one of the most difficult texts in all the Scriptures, he said, to interpret properly.
setting before them as exemplars in the religious life those very worshippers of Mammon
he was their spiritual accountant

questions.prompt: The story is called “Grace.” Where, if anywhere, does grace appear?
facilitatorNotes: In theology grace is God’s free, unearned gift. In the story the word has meant the grace of a silk hat and Mr. Fogarty’s grace of manner; here it is a phrase in a bookkeeper’s formula. A defensible reading is that the story shows grace reduced to accounts; others argue that the plain admission “I find this wrong” keeps its possibility open.
evidence: But, with God's grace, I will rectify this and this.
to be straight and manly with God

questions.prompt: Joyce’s brother said the story’s three parts follow Dante’s journey from Hell through Purgatory to Paradise. How well does this last scene play the part of Paradise?
facilitatorNotes: The fall to the lavatory floor and the sickbed fit Hell and Purgatory comically. Paradise is a church of black coats and white collars and a sermon that ends in balanced accounts. The parallel sharpens the irony; readers can argue whether the ending is pure satire or holds some real hope.
evidence: The light of the lamps of the church fell upon an assembly of black clothes and white collars
Well, I have verified my accounts. I find all well.
